classification.difficultyReason: The parts supply the diagonal vectors, perpendicular side product and squared magnitude before a routine dot-product expansion and geometric interpretation.

content.prompt:
The square $ABCD$ to the right has side length $\ell$.

Let $\overrightarrow{AB}=\underset{\sim}{a}$ and $\overrightarrow{BC}=\underset{\sim}{b}$.

spec.description: An unshaded upright square with all four referenced vertex labels outside it and the side-length label below AB. Source grey outline is rendered in house black.
spec.mathematics: A is bottom left, B bottom right, C top right and D top left; AB has length ell. No diagonals or angle markers are supplied.
spec.answerVisibility: Always visible; contains only supplied geometry and givens.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Express $\overrightarrow{AC}$ and $\overrightarrow{BD}$ in terms of $\underset{\sim}{a}$ and $\underset{\sim}{b}$.

answer.worked:
$$\underset{\sim}{a}\cdot\underset{\sim}{b}=|\underset{\sim}{a}||\underset{\sim}{b}|\cos\theta$$

Here $\theta$ is the angle between $\underset{\sim}{a}$ and $\underset{\sim}{b}$. Since $ABCD$ is a square, $\theta=90^\circ$, $|\underset{\sim}{a}|=\ell$ and $|\underset{\sim}{b}|=\ell$.

$$\begin{aligned}\underset{\sim}{a}\cdot\underset{\sim}{b}&=\ell\times\ell\times\cos90^\circ\\&=0\end{aligned}$$

By Pythagoras,

$$\begin{aligned}|\underset{\sim}{a}+\underset{\sim}{b}|^2&=|\overrightarrow{AC}|^2\\&=\ell^2+\ell^2\\&=2\ell^2\\|\overrightarrow{AC}|&=\sqrt{2\ell^2}=\sqrt2\,\ell\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}|\underset{\sim}{b}-\underset{\sim}{a}|^2&=|\overrightarrow{BD}|^2\\&=\ell^2+\ell^2\\|\overrightarrow{BD}|&=\sqrt{2\ell^2}=\sqrt2\,\ell\end{aligned}$$

Using the distributive and commutative properties of the dot product,

$$\begin{aligned}(\underset{\sim}{a}+\underset{\sim}{b})\cdot(\underset{\sim}{b}-\underset{\sim}{a})&=\underset{\sim}{a}\cdot\underset{\sim}{b}-\underset{\sim}{a}\cdot\underset{\sim}{a}+\underset{\sim}{b}\cdot\underset{\sim}{b}-\underset{\sim}{b}\cdot\underset{\sim}{a}\\&=0-\ell^2+\ell^2-0\\&=0\end{aligned}$$

children.label: e
children.prompt: What have we proven in part d about the diagonals of a square?

answer.short: The diagonals of a square meet at right angles.
answer.worked: From part a, the diagonals have vectors $\overrightarrow{AC}=\underset{\sim}{a}+\underset{\sim}{b}$ and $\overrightarrow{BD}=\underset{\sim}{b}-\underset{\sim}{a}$. Their dot product is zero by part d, so the diagonals are perpendicular.
